source: Aligned to College Board AP Biology Course and Exam Description (effective Fall 2025)

units.title: Chemistry of Life
review_notes: Life depends on the chemical properties of water: polarity, hydrogen bonding, cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, high heat of vaporization, and ice being less dense than liquid water.
Hydrogen bonds are weak individually but powerful collectively; they stabilize water properties, DNA base pairing, and protein structure.
Carbon is central because it can form four covalent bonds, allowing diverse organic molecules and complex carbon skeletons.
Functional groups determine many molecule properties: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, amino, sulfhydryl, phosphate, and methyl.
Biological macromolecules are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids; structure determines function.
Carbohydrates include monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides. Starch and glycogen are energy storage; cellulose and chitin are structural.
Lipids are hydrophobic and include triglycerides, phospholipids, and steroids. Phospholipids are amphipathic and form membranes.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Their function depends on shape, which depends on primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure.
Denaturation changes protein shape and function, often due to pH, salinity, or temperature changes.
Nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information. DNA and RNA are built from nucleotides containing a sugar, phosphate group, and nitrogenous base.
Dehydration synthesis builds polymers by removing water; hydrolysis breaks polymers by adding water.
Structure-function relationships are constant exam territory: saturated vs unsaturated fats, alpha vs beta glucose linkages, amino acid side chains, and nucleotide sequence effects.
dont_mix_these_up: Hydrogen bond vs covalent bond: hydrogen bonds are weaker intermolecular or intramolecular attractions; covalent bonds share electrons.
Monomer vs polymer: monomers are subunits; polymers are chains of subunits.
Dehydration synthesis vs hydrolysis: dehydration builds; hydrolysis breaks.
Saturated vs unsaturated fat: saturated has no double bonds and is straighter; unsaturated has one or more double bonds and kinked chains.
Starch/glycogen vs cellulose: starch and glycogen use alpha glucose for storage; cellulose uses beta glucose for structure.
DNA vs RNA: DNA usually has deoxyribose and thymine; RNA usually has ribose and uracil.

units.title: Cells
review_notes: Cells are the basic units of life. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus; eukaryotes have both.
Surface area-to-volume ratio limits cell size. As a cell gets larger, volume increases faster than surface area, making transport less efficient.
Membranes are selectively permeable and follow the fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol, and carbohydrates.
Membrane permeability depends on size, charge, polarity, and transport proteins. Small nonpolar molecules cross more easily than ions and large polar molecules.
Passive transport requires no energy input: diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion move substances down their concentration gradient.
Active transport requires energy to move substances against a gradient, often through membrane pumps or cotransport proteins.
Water potential predicts water movement. Water moves from higher water potential to lower water potential.
Tonicity compares solute concentrations and predicts net water movement: hypotonic, hypertonic, isotonic.

Organelles have structure-function relationships: nucleus stores DNA; ribosomes make proteins; rough ER modifies proteins; smooth ER makes lipids; Golgi sorts and ships; lysosomes digest; mitochondria make ATP; chloroplasts perform photosynthesis.
Compartmentalization increases efficiency by separating incompatible processes and concentrating reactants and enzymes.
Endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts from engulfed prokaryotes; evidence includes double membranes, circular DNA, ribosomes, and binary fission-like replication.
Disruptions to membrane transport, organelles, or SA:V relationships commonly appear in experimental and graph questions.
dont_mix_these_up: Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic: prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have them.
Diffusion vs osmosis: diffusion is movement of any particles down a gradient; osmosis is specifically water movement.
Facilitated diffusion vs active transport: facilitated diffusion uses proteins but no ATP; active transport moves against the gradient and requires energy.
Hypertonic/hypotonic: hypertonic solution has higher solute concentration relative to the cell; hypotonic has lower.
Concentration gradient vs electrochemical gradient: concentration considers solute amount only; electrochemical includes charge.
Plasmolysis vs lysis: plasmolysis is membrane pulling from the wall in plants; lysis is bursting, often in animal cells.

units.title: Cellular Energetics
review_notes: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower activation energy but do not change the overall free energy change of a reaction.
Enzyme activity depends on active site shape, substrate concentration, temperature, pH, and regulatory molecules such as inhibitors or activators.
Competitive inhibitors bind the active site; noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and alter enzyme shape.
ATP is the immediate energy currency of the cell; energy is released when ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and phosphate.
Photosynthesis captures light energy: light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and produce ATP, NADPH, and O2; the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma and fixes CO2 into sugar.

Cellular respiration harvests energy from organic molecules: glycolysis in the cytosol, pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Redox reactions drive electron transfer. Electron carriers such as NADH and FADH2 deliver high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain.
Chemiosmosis uses a proton gradient and ATP synthase to make ATP; this is central to both oxidative phosphorylation and photophosphorylation.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ when oxygen is absent, allowing glycolysis to continue but producing much less ATP than aerobic respiration.
The connection between structure and process matters: cristae increase ETC surface area, thylakoids separate compartments for proton gradients, and membrane permeability is crucial.
Experimental questions often test how changing pH, temperature, substrate amount, light wavelength, carbon dioxide, or oxygen affects rates of enzyme function, photosynthesis, or respiration.
dont_mix_these_up: Activation energy vs free energy change: enzymes lower activation energy, not ΔG.
Competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition: competitive blocks the active site; noncompetitive changes enzyme shape elsewhere.
Photosynthesis vs cellular respiration: photosynthesis stores energy in sugars; respiration releases energy from sugars.
Light-dependent reactions vs Calvin cycle: light reactions make ATP/NADPH and O2; Calvin cycle uses ATP/NADPH to fix carbon.
Substrate-level phosphorylation vs oxidative phosphorylation: substrate-level transfers phosphate directly; oxidative uses ETC and chemiosmosis.
Aerobic respiration vs fermentation: aerobic uses oxygen as final electron acceptor and yields much more ATP.

units.title: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle
review_notes: Cells communicate through direct contact, local signaling, and long-distance signaling; the response depends on receptor presence and signal transduction pathways.
Ligands bind receptors specifically. Major receptor types include G protein-coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases, and intracellular receptors.
Signal transduction commonly involves reception, transduction, and response. Cascades amplify signals so one ligand can trigger a large cellular effect.
Second messengers such as cAMP, calcium ions, and IP3 relay intracellular signals and help amplify responses.
Phosphorylation cascades regulate protein activity by adding or removing phosphate groups; kinases add phosphates and phosphatases remove them.
Positive and negative feedback regulate homeostasis. Negative feedback stabilizes a system; positive feedback amplifies a change until a defined endpoint.
The cell cycle includes G1, S, G2, and M phases. DNA is replicated in S phase; mitosis and cytokinesis occur in M phase.
Cell cycle checkpoints help prevent division of damaged cells. Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases regulate progression.
Disruption of checkpoint control can lead to cancer. Proto-oncogenes normally promote regulated growth; when mutated they can become oncogenes. Tumor suppressor genes help restrain division.
Mitosis produces genetically similar daughter cells for growth and repair. Errors in regulation or chromosome separation can have major consequences.
Exam questions often combine models, signaling diagrams, mutations, and predictions about how altering one pathway component changes the final response.
dont_mix_these_up: Signal reception vs transduction vs response: reception is ligand-receptor binding; transduction relays the signal; response is the cellular effect.
GPCR vs RTK: GPCR activates G proteins; RTK dimerizes and autophosphorylates tyrosines.
Kinase vs phosphatase: kinases add phosphate groups; phosphatases remove them.
Positive vs negative feedback: positive amplifies deviation; negative reduces deviation.
Mitosis vs cytokinesis: mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
Proto-oncogene vs tumor suppressor gene: proto-oncogenes promote controlled growth; tumor suppressors restrain it.

units.title: Heredity
review_notes: Meiosis creates haploid gametes and increases genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.
Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I; sister chromatids separate in meiosis II. Reduction to haploid occurs when homologs separate.
Fertilization restores diploidy and creates new allele combinations.
Mendelian inheritance explains segregation and independent assortment, but many traits show more complex inheritance patterns.
Probability rules apply to inheritance problems, including monohybrid and dihybrid crosses.
Linked genes do not assort independently; recombination frequency can be used to estimate map distance on chromosomes.
Pedigrees help infer inheritance patterns such as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, and mitochondrial.
Chromosomal errors such as nondisjunction can produce abnormal chromosome numbers, including aneuploidy.
Sources of genetic variation include mutation, crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilization.
Phenotype results from genotype and environment, and gene expression patterns can modify trait outcomes.
The exam often punishes loose thinking about meiosis stages, chromosome number, and whether a question is testing genes, alleles, chromosomes, or chromatids.
dont_mix_these_up: Homologous chromosomes vs sister chromatids: homologs are similar chromosomes from different parents; sister chromatids are identical copies after DNA replication.
Meiosis I vs meiosis II: meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Gene vs allele: a gene is a DNA sequence affecting a trait; an allele is a variant of that gene.
Genotype vs phenotype: genotype is allele combination; phenotype is observable expression.
Independent assortment vs crossing over: independent assortment is random homolog orientation; crossing over exchanges segments between homologs.
Autosomal vs sex-linked inheritance: autosomal genes are on non-sex chromosomes; sex-linked genes are on X or Y.

units.title: Gene Expression and Regulation
review_notes: DNA structure explains information storage: antiparallel strands, complementary base pairing, and a sugar-phosphate backbone.
DNA replication is semiconservative. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end, so synthesis proceeds 5' to 3'. Leading and lagging strands differ because of antiparallel structure.
Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; in eukaryotes, RNA processing includes 5' capping, poly-A tail addition, and intron removal by splicing.
Translation occurs at ribosomes. mRNA codons are read 5' to 3', and tRNA anticodons deliver amino acids to build a polypeptide.
Mutations can be silent, missense, nonsense, insertion, or deletion; frameshifts often have large effects.
Gene expression can be regulated at many levels: chromatin structure, transcription, RNA processing, mRNA stability, translation, and post-translational modification.
Prokaryotic gene regulation often uses operons such as lac and trp. Eukaryotic regulation involves transcription factors, enhancers, silencers, and epigenetic modification.
DNA methylation and histone modification affect chromatin accessibility and therefore transcription.
Differential gene expression explains cell specialization; cells can share the same genome but express different genes.
Biotechnology topics include restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis, PCR, DNA sequencing, plasmids, transformation, and CRISPR-based editing.
This unit is trap-heavy because the exam expects precise directionality, strand logic, and regulation mechanisms rather than vague 'DNA makes protein' summaries.
dont_mix_these_up: Coding strand vs template strand: RNA matches the coding strand except U replaces T, but RNA is built using the template strand.
Transcription vs translation: transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation makes protein from mRNA.
Replication vs transcription: replication copies DNA; transcription makes RNA from one DNA region.
Introns vs exons: introns are removed from pre-mRNA; exons remain in mature mRNA.
Enhancer/silencer vs transcription factor: enhancer and silencer are DNA sequences; transcription factors are proteins that bind them.
DNA methylation vs histone acetylation: methylation often reduces transcription; acetylation usually opens chromatin and increases transcription.

units.title: Natural Selection
review_notes: Evolution is change in allele frequencies in a population over time. Individuals do not evolve; populations do.
Natural selection requires heritable variation and differential reproductive success. It acts on phenotypes but changes populations genetically across generations.
Evidence for evolution includes fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography, direct observation, and molecular homology.
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a null model for a non-evolving population: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, and no natural selection.
Microevolution can result from mutation, natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, and nonrandom mating.
Genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance and is strongest in small populations; founder effect and bottleneck effect are classic examples.
Selection patterns include directional, stabilizing, and disruptive selection.
Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated. Prezygotic barriers prevent mating or fertilization; postzygotic barriers reduce hybrid success.
Allopatric speciation involves geographic isolation; sympatric speciation occurs without physical separation, often through polyploidy, habitat differentiation, or nonrandom mating.
Phylogeny reconstructs evolutionary relationships. Cladograms use shared derived characters to infer common ancestry, and outgroups help identify primitive vs derived traits.
This unit gets overtested because it connects population genetics, speciation, and evidence into one logic chain instead of separate fact piles.
dont_mix_these_up: Natural selection vs genetic drift: selection is nonrandom and tied to fitness; drift is random and strongest in small populations.
Gene flow vs genetic drift: gene flow moves alleles between populations; drift changes frequencies by chance within a population.
Analogous vs homologous structures: analogous reflect convergent evolution; homologous reflect common ancestry.
Prezygotic vs postzygotic isolation: prezygotic acts before fertilization; postzygotic acts after fertilization.
Allopatric vs sympatric speciation: allopatric requires geographic isolation; sympatric does not.
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium vs evolution: equilibrium means allele frequencies stay constant; evolution means they change.

units.title: Ecology
review_notes: Ecology studies interactions among organisms and between organisms and their environment across multiple scales: organism, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere.
Population dynamics depend on births, deaths, immigration, emigration, and environmental limits. Exponential growth occurs with abundant resources; logistic growth includes carrying capacity.
r-selected species generally mature quickly, produce many offspring, and thrive in unstable environments; K-selected species invest more in fewer offspring in more stable environments.
Communities are shaped by species interactions: competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism.
Niche refers to a species' role and resource use. Competitive exclusion states that two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely in the same place.
Energy flows while matter cycles. Trophic levels transfer only a small portion of energy upward, producing pyramids of productivity, biomass, or numbers.
Primary productivity depends on photosynthetic rate; gross primary productivity minus respiration equals net primary productivity.
Biogeochemical cycles move water and key elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus through biotic and abiotic reservoirs.
Human activities affect ecosystems through climate change, eutrophication, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, overharvesting, and altered nutrient cycling.
Experimental ecology questions often require interpreting graphs, carrying capacity changes, survivorship patterns, and whether a variable is density-dependent or density-independent.
You need mechanism, not slogans: know why populations level off, why energy decreases across trophic levels, and how disruptions propagate through systems.
dont_mix_these_up: Exponential vs logistic growth: exponential is J-shaped with no effective limits; logistic is S-shaped and approaches carrying capacity.
Density-dependent vs density-independent factors: density-dependent effects strengthen as population size rises; density-independent factors affect populations regardless of density.
Food chain vs food web: a food chain is one pathway; a food web is many interconnected pathways.
Gross primary productivity vs net primary productivity: NPP = GPP - respiration.
Matter cycles vs energy flow: matter is recycled; energy flows and is lost as heat.
r-selected vs K-selected: r favors many low-investment offspring; K favors fewer high-investment offspring.
